# After Cai Guo-Qiang's *Sky Ladder*

Quick, before the sun rises—rise once more, my grandmother. The artist won't mind if you borrow his ladder to the sky. Place your foot upon the lowest rung and climb still higher, even though you are but a skeleton, your neck broken from that fall down the stairs on Guy Fawkes night. The ladder is bound in gunpowder, and he has already lit the fuse. Your bones ascend now like firecrackers taking flight. You are half a kilometer high, halfway to the universe, my joy-gardener.

I hope you find a garden there, its soil black and rich enough for your black roses—hybrids, like you: half white, half Indian; half woman, half flower; their roots twining through your skull, you who were once transplanted among the pale roses of a British family. Your skin is now a blend of photons and soot.

What do you discover up there? Is there a hothouse waiting? Do alien hands, deft with their brushes, pollinate the stars? Do you recall how your tomatoes kept yielding more and more planets? Are there now constellations of exotic fruit, now that you've reached the summit? Have you traveled far enough back through space and time to find yourself alive again?

The ladder has burned to char; the hot air balloon that held it aloft begins to collapse. The explosions have ended. Cai showers his head with champagne, while his hundred-year-old grandmother watches on, through the small screen of her phone.

*Did you see it?* he asks. *Did you hear the whoosh, the rat-tat-tat at heaven's starry door?*

You may go back to sleep now.

**After Cai Guo-Qiang's "Sky Ladder"**

Rise once more, grandmother mine, in these hours before dawn breaks. The artist surely wouldn't object to you making use of his ladder to heaven. Set your foot upon its lowest step and continue upward, though your neck lies broken and your body reduced to bone from that tumble down the stairs on the night of Guy Fawkes. Gunpowder coats every rung of that ladder, and the fuse has already caught fire. Your skeleton climbs like a lit firework. Half a kilometer into the sky already—you're halfway to the cosmos now, my cultivator of happiness. May you discover soil there, dark and fertile enough to nourish your black roses—for you were always a hybrid too, part white, part Indian, part woman, part blossom, with roots winding through your very skull, having been grafted long ago into a British family's garden of pale petals. Your flesh has transformed into something made of light particles and ash.

What awaits you at such heights? Does a greenhouse exist up there? Do otherworldly fingers, gentle with tiny brushes, spread pollen between the stars? Do you recall those tomato vines that somehow kept producing new worlds instead of fruit? Now that you've reached the summit, do strange fruits hang like constellations? Has this journey carried you far enough through time and space to return you to the days when you still breathed?

The ladder has burned to char, and the balloon that once held it aloft begins to sag and fall. The fireworks have finished their display. Cai pours champagne over his own head in celebration, while his grandmother—a century old—observes everything through the screen of a phone. "Did you catch it?" he calls out to her. "Did that whooshing sound reach you, that rapid knocking against heaven's door?"

Now, you may return to your rest.

# Ascending Through Fire: A Study of Memory, Heritage, and Transformation

This poem performs a remarkable act of artistic alchemy, borrowing the image of Cai Guo-Qiang's famous pyrotechnic installation "Sky Ladder"—a hundred-meter ladder of fire that blazed against the dawn sky in 2015—and repurposing it as a mythic vessel for personal grief and reconciliation. Where Cai's original work was conceived as a tribute to his own grandmother, the poem appropriates this gesture and refracts it through the speaker's own loss, creating a layered meditation on death, identity, and ascension.

## The Grandmother's Fiery Resurrection

At the poem's emotional core lies the grandmother herself, rendered with unflinching physicality as a skeleton bearing the mark of her death—a broken neck, the result of a fatal fall down a staircase. This is no sanitized image of peaceful passing; the poem insists on the brutal reality of the body's failure. Yet from this stark image of mortality, the poem stages an act of reclamation: the grandmother's bones climb the gunpowder-wrapped rungs of the ladder, and as she ascends, her skeletal frame ignites like a string of firecrackers. The imagery is startling in its juxtaposition of violence and celebration—the same combustive force that might destroy is here repurposed as the very mechanism of her liberation, transforming a body broken by falling into one now propelled upward in light and flame.

## A Hybrid Identity in Bloom

The grandmother is further characterized through a series of doublings that speak to the complexities of mixed heritage and belonging. She exists as half white, half Indian; half woman, half flower—an embodiment that resists singular categorization. Her identity is symbolized through black roses, a striking departure from the pale, conventional roses of the British family into which she married or belonged. This floral imagery does more than decorate; it roots her difference in something organic and living, suggesting that her hybridity was not a fracture but a distinct and vital form of growth, dark and singular against a garden of uniform pallor. The "rootedness" attributed to her suggests that despite dislocation, despite the fall, despite death itself, she remains connected to something enduring—her own nature, her own soil.

## Imagining the Afterlife

The poem's speaker, caught in the aftermath of loss, turns to wonder and speculation about what awaits the grandmother beyond the threshold of death. The questions posed are deliberately surreal and expansive: celestial gardens where the ordinary laws of botany might not apply, constellations shaped like exotic fruits scattered across the heavens, and perhaps most poignantly, the possibility that she might return—not literally, but in memory or spirit—to a single moment when she was still alive. This speculative gesture allows the poem to hover between mourning and hope, refusing to settle into either despair or easy comfort. The afterlife imagined here is not a fixed paradise but a space of continued strangeness and wonder, as unpredictable and vivid as the grandmother herself.

## Blurring Fact and Invention

In its final movement, the poem performs its most sophisticated maneuver: a return to the real-world context of Cai Guo-Qiang's artwork, specifically the detail that his actual hundred-year-old grandmother watched the ladder's fiery ascent via video call, unable to be present in person. This factual anchor collides with the poem's invented grandmother, and the boundary between the two women—one real, one imagined, one the artist's, one the speaker's—begins to dissolve. This blurring is not a failure of clarity but a deliberate act of poetic fusion, suggesting that all grandmothers, all losses, all acts of familial love and tribute might be, in some sense, the same gesture repeated across different lives. The poem closes with a tender act of release: an address to the grandmother granting her permission to rest once more, the fire spent, the ladder climbed, the wondering momentarily stilled. This final tenderness transforms the entire poem into an elegy that has, through its own imaginative fire, found a way to let go.

# Sky Ladder for Grandmother

*after Cai Guo-Qiang*

The ladder ignites against the dark harbor,
five hundred feet of gold fire climbing
where no ladder should be able to climb—
a spine of light stitched between
water and stars, and I think of you,
grandmother, who never saw such things,
who knew only the slow combustion
of roses opening in Ohio summers,
their petals the color of something
between your two bloods: the pale
Scottish stock of your father, the deep
autumnal brown of your mother's people,
whose names were taken along with
so much else, whose faces you carried
folded into the corners of your own.

You who pressed seeds into black earth
with the same hands that braided
my mother's hair, who spoke of England
and reservation both in hushed tones,
as if uncertain which ghost
you were allowed to claim—

I want to tell you the ladder is for you.

I want to say: climb, the way you climbed
out of whatever confusion made you
half of two worlds and whole of neither,
the way your roses climbed the trellis
you built with your own broken-knuckled hands,
red and white and red-and-white
blooming into a language
no one had to translate.

The fire only lasts for minutes.
Cai's ladder curls into smoke,
its rungs dissolving into the same air
that swallowed you three years ago
in a hospital room the color of old rain.
But watch how the crowd holds
its collective breath, how even
disappearance can look like ascension
if you catch it at the right angle—

Grandmother, I am trying to build you
a ladder out of memory,
out of grainy photographs
where you stand smiling among your roses,
squinting into a sun
that has long since set.

I am trying to say: you were the ladder.
You were the fire climbing between
two countries of blood,
two silences, two names
you carried like matches
you were afraid to strike.

Now the sky exhales its brief gold answer
and I stand here, aching,
watching everything beautiful
undo itself into dark,
believing—because I have to believe something—
that somewhere in that scattering light
you are still climbing,
still reaching the place
where all our contradictions
finally catch and hold,

blooming like the roses you left behind,
red as a wound, white as forgiveness,
climbing toward whatever heaven
would have you, whole,
at last, at last.

# After Cai and Guo: The Fall of Two Ancient States

In the complex political landscape of ancient China, the states of Cai and Guo occupied significant positions during the Zhou dynasty period. Their eventual fates offer valuable insight into the shifting power dynamics that characterized this era of Chinese history.

## The State of Guo

Guo was one of the vassal states established during the early Zhou dynasty, strategically positioned to serve as a defensive buffer for the royal domain. For generations, Guo maintained relative stability, its rulers navigating the complex web of alliances and obligations that bound the feudal states together. However, as central Zhou authority weakened, Guo found itself increasingly vulnerable to the ambitions of more powerful neighboring states.

## The State of Cai

Similarly, Cai emerged as another important vassal territory, its rulers tracing descent from Zhou nobility. Cai's location placed it at the crossroads of competing interests among the larger regional powers, particularly as the era of the Spring and Autumn period brought intensified competition among the states vying for supremacy.

## After the Decline

What happened after these states began losing their independence illustrates a broader pattern in Chinese antiquity. As larger, more militarily capable states like Chu, Jin, and Qin expanded their influence, smaller states like Cai and Guo became targets for annexation or reduced to vassal status under stronger patrons. Their absorption into larger political entities reflected the gradual consolidation of power that would eventually culminate in the unification of China.

The stories of Cai and Guo, though smaller chapters in the grand narrative of ancient Chinese history, demonstrate how even established, legitimate states could not withstand the tides of political transformation. Their legacies persist primarily through historical records and the surnames that many descendants carry to this day, connecting modern individuals to these ancient political entities that once played their part in shaping Chinese civilization.

The transition from independent statehood to absorption into larger polities represents a recurring theme throughout Chinese history, one that the experiences of Cai and Guo exemplify particularly well.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal elegy for my mixed-race grandmother (half English, half Indian) who died falling down the stairs on Bonfire Night, using Cai Guo-Qiang's "Sky Ladder" artwork as its central image.
counterfactuals.output:
**Sky Ladder for My Grandmother**

They say Cai Guo-Qiang waited fifteen years
for windless weather, for a sky
still enough to hold a ladder made of fire —
five hundred feet of flame unrolling upward
from a hot air balloon at dawn,
each rung igniting the one below it,
climbing into cloud like a wound that heals
backwards, like a fall reversed.

I think of this because you fell downward,
Grandmother, on the fifth of November,
the night the whole of England
apologizes for its history with light —
effigies and gunpowder, chrysanthemum shells
blooming over rooftops in Sussex red and gold,
the same week, some years, that Lakshmi's diyas
would have flickered at your mother's door
in Lucknow, in another life, in the life
you carried folded like a sari
underneath your English cardigan.

The stairs were carpeted. That's the detail
no one wants: the ordinary softness
of a thing that could not save you.
Bannister, hip, the small brass stair-rod
you polished every Sunday with a rag
that smelled of Brasso and cardamom —
how the body finds its own geometry
of falling, the way flame finds
its ladder rung by rung by instinct,
not by plan.

I want to give you Cai's fire instead of gravity.
I want to lace a hundred silk-white rungs
from the foot of your staircase to the sky
you were always half-facing —
one eye on Surrey drizzle,
one on Ganges light —
and let combustion carry you
the way it carries paper lanterns,
the way it carried Guy Fawkes' effigy
each year while, four thousand miles away,
your grandmother lit oil in clay bowls
for a goddess of wealth and safe returns.

Both fires wanted you to rise.
Both fires, that night, were only doing
what fire does — 
it does not know whose ancestors it echoes,
it only knows it must go up or out.

So let the ladder be lit for you now,
retroactively, into the dark
above that carpeted staircase,
that domestic Everest, that small
unglamorous cliff where an ordinary Tuesday
became your last geography.
Let the balloon lift the rope of flame
so slowly the neighbors mistake it
for a firework that forgot to end,
and let you climb it backwards from the bottom stair,
sari-silk and Woolworth's slippers,
half your mouth still saying *beta*,
half still saying *love* —

up through the smoke that smells of sulphur and of ghee,
up past the year you left Lucknow,
up past the year you buried your accent
in a Surrey semi-detached,
up into whatever sky holds both
your histories without asking
which one is a costume
and which one is the skin.

There is no photograph of this.
There was no wind that night either way.
But I have decided the ladder was real,
that combustion is a kind of grace,
that somewhere above the cul-de-sac
you are still climbing,
each rung a small controlled disaster,
each spark a diya,
each diya a bonfire,
each bonfire, briefly, unbearably,
you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem titled "After Cai Guo-Qiang" that reimagines the artist's fireworks ladder installation as a path for a deceased grandmother's skeleton to ascend into the cosmos.
counterfactuals.output:
# After Cai Guo-Qiang

They built the ladder out of fire—
five hundred feet of gold combustion
climbing nothing, climbing air,
a bridge that burns behind its own arrival.

I think of you, Grandmother, small-boned,
folded now into the earth like a letter
no one has opened yet.

If they could rig a ladder from your bed
of clay and buried buttons,
if the sparks could find the gaps
between your vertebrae and light them
one by one—an ascending morse code,
*I was here, I was here, I was here*—

would you climb it, wrapped in nothing
but the memory of your good wool coat?

Your skeleton knows only stillness now,
the long math of settling,
calcium letting go of its grip on shape.
But bone is just a kind of ladder too,
each rung a year, a labor,
a child raised, a garden kept,
the femur long as any story
you told me twice because the first time
I was too young to hold it.

I imagine you rising rung by rung of smoke,
your ribs catching updrafts like a kite's spine,
your skull tipped back to face the ones
who left before you did—
the dead make constellations
out of loneliness, don't they?
They must. What else explains
the way stars cluster into shapes
we call by names we love?

Cai's ladder disappeared in ninety seconds.
Grief takes longer. It rebuilds itself
each night in different colors,
a private, unrecorded pyrotechnics
no one else can see.

But if I squint at the dark above the hills
where you are not, and never will be, buried—
I can make the fire.
I can make the ladder.
I can make you climb.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: I need a prose poem blending grief, gardening imagery (black roses, tomatoes turning into planets), and the real story of Cai Guo-Qiang's grandmother watching his sky ladder piece on her phone—can you write something that merges my own grandmother's death with this artwork?
counterfactuals.output:
# The Ladder

My grandmother died the way tomatoes ripen on the vine when no one is watching—slowly, then all at once, red deepening to something planetary, something with its own gravity and weather systems. I found her garden three weeks later, the black roses she'd grown from stubbornness and spite still holding their color like held breath, like a secret about how dark things can bloom anyway.

Cai Guo-Qiang built a ladder of fire that touched the sky over Quanzhou, five hundred meters of gold sparks climbing toward nothing, toward everything, and his grandmother—one hundred years old, too frail to leave her bed—watched it happen on a phone screen, the whole burning ascension compressed into something small enough to hold in her failing hands. I think about this: how we bring the sky down to the size of what our grandmothers can still touch. How fire becomes small enough for dying fingers to trace.

My grandmother's phone sat unused on her nightstand for the last year of her life. I never showed her anything on it. I never thought to bring the sky down to her size, to compress some burning ladder into the space between her palms. Instead I brought her tomatoes from the garden, still warm, and she'd hold them like small planets, like worlds she'd made from dirt and water and the stubborn insistence of green things.

The tomatoes are still turning in the garden she left behind. No one there to pick them. They swell and redden and become their own solar systems, indifferent to grief, indifferent to ladders or fire or any human architecture of ascension. This is what growing things do—they don't wait for us to finish dying before they finish living.

I think of Cai's grandmother watching that fire-ladder disappear into smoke and sky, the artwork itself designed to vanish, to become only residue and memory and a story someone tells later. My grandmother's roses are like this too—black not because they mourn but because black is just a color, is just a chemical accident of anthocyanins, is just a flower being a flower regardless of what we need it to mean.

I want to build her a ladder. I want five hundred meters of something bright enough to reach whatever place holds her now, some structure of fire and gold that could compress the enormous fact of her absence into something small enough to hold in trembling hands, something I could watch on a screen from the safety of this side of dying.

Instead: tomatoes ripening into small red worlds. Black roses holding their impossible color. A garden continuing its quiet green work without permission, without grief, without any ladder at all—just soil and light and the terrible, ordinary miracle of things continuing to grow after everything that mattered has already burned away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental elegy addressed directly to "you," a grandmother who was a florist or gardener of mixed heritage, incorporating fireworks, space imagery, and the true anecdote of Cai Guo-Qiang lighting his ladder for his 100-year-old grandmother.
counterfactuals.output:
**Sky Ladder, For You**

*i.*

You, who grafted white peony onto red rootstock
because the catalog said *incompatible*
and you said *watch me*—

grandmother, half a world folded into your wrists,
Cantonese vowels pressed flat under an English mouth,
a name that changed at three different borders—

I am writing this the way you used to graft:
cut here, bind there, wait for the green to forget
it was ever two things.

*ii.*

In 2015 a man named Cai Guo-Qiang
built a ladder out of fire
five hundred meters tall,
gunpowder stitched to a hot air balloon
so it could climb straight up from Huiyu Island
into the pre-dawn dark—

he lit it for his grandmother.
She was one hundred years old
and watching from a screen
because her body could no longer come outside
to see the sky do something new.

He said: *I wanted to give her a gift
before it was too late to give her anything.*

*iii.*

You did not get a ladder of fire.
You got a hospital window
facing a parking lot,
one dying ficus someone forgot to water,
and me, learning too late
which of your stories were true
and which were grafted on
to make the losses climb a little higher.

*iv.*

Still—you were a kind of pyrotechnician.

Every bulb you buried was a small delayed
detonation, timed to bloom
months after your hands had let it go—
tulips going off like flares in April,
dahlias in September holding their fire
until the exact hour of frost.

You knew how to plant something
that would explode into color
long after you'd walked away from the dirt.

*v.*

I keep thinking of the ladder standing there
against the last of the night,
a hundred thousand golden sparks
running up its rungs like something
finally deciding to be a comet
instead of falling—

grandmother, I would build you that.
I would burn a staircase into the sky
and walk you up it rung by rung,
past the ficus, past the parking lot,
past the border guards who mispronounced you,
until the graft finally took
and there was only one thing left of you,
blooming,

visible from very far away,
the way a star is really
just a flower we agreed to call by another name.

*vi.*

He watched his ladder collapse into embers
after only two and a half minutes.
Someone said *is that all,*
and he said *that was never the point—
the point was that she saw it.*

*vii.*

So let this be the ladder I light for you,
however small, however late:
a hundred words instead of a hundred years,
climbing nowhere, burning out fast,
visible, I hope, from wherever you're arranged now—
some garden past the atmosphere
where every hybrid finally holds,
where mixed things are not called wrong,
only *rare*,

and the sky, your last and strangest greenhouse,
keeps blooming you back to me
in light that left its source
long before I knew enough
to call it grief.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical, dreamlike piece about death and ascension that fuses personal family history with Cai Guo-Qiang's "Sky Ladder," using motifs of gunpowder, roses, and stars to explore mixed identity and mourning.
counterfactuals.output:
# Sky Ladder for My Grandmother

The gunpowder remembers everything, they say—
each grain a small held breath, a syllable
waiting for fire to give it voice.

My grandmother crossed an ocean once
with a name that changed its shape
in every mouth that tried to hold it,
the way a rose changes color
depending on the hour you cut it,
depending on who is doing the cutting.

I think of Cai's ladder, that impossible
gold spine unrolling into sky above the harbor
where his own grandmother waited, ninety-nine
and dying, wanting only to see
what fire could build toward heaven
before she went there herself.

Five hundred meters of flame
climbing like a live thing,
climbing like every ancestor
who ever wanted proof
that the distance between earth and elsewhere
could be measured, could be built,
plank by burning plank.

*

In my family we do not speak of dying.
We speak instead of journeys, of the sea
my grandmother crossed twice—
once forward, once in memory,
her accent softening like a rose
left too long in water, petals
translating themselves into a language
of falling.

She kept dried flowers in a drawer
the way some keep photographs,
the way Cai keeps gunpowder
in jars labeled by color, by hour,
by what he hopes the burning will become.

*

Half of me is smoke from a country
I have only visited in her stories.
Half of me is the silence after,
the ash that settles like snow
that never learned how to be cold.

This is the mixed inheritance:
one hand holding matches,
one hand holding roses,
never quite sure
which will bloom first,
which will simply burn.

*

When she died, I imagined a ladder—
not gold, not fire, but something
built from all her unspoken names,
each rung a syllable
she swallowed to make room
for a new country's tongue.

I imagined her climbing,
finally weightless,
finally unburdened
by translation,
her body turning slowly
into stars,
into the kind of light
that takes so long to reach us
we call it *ancient*
and mean *still arriving*.

*

Cai says gunpowder is not destruction
but a kind of prayer—
each explosion a flower
blooming backward into brightness,
each spark a small rebellion
against the ordinary dark.

I want to believe this
about grief too:
that mourning is not the ending
but the ignition,
that somewhere my grandmother
is still climbing,
still becoming
the ladder and the sky
and the fire that built them both,

still arriving,
still a rose
unfurling
into stars.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
